sections.title: 1. Thread Startup, Lifetime & Cancellation Tricks
sections.description: Preventing nullptr races at startup, dangling references, and broken stopRequested() loops.

blocks.title: Trick #1: The Starting Wall (*Barrière de démarrage*)
blocks.content:
**The Problem:** In `main()`, you spawn `N` threads in a loop and store their pointers in `threads[i]`. If Thread 0 starts running immediately and calls `stop_threads()` (iterating over `threads`) before `main()` finishes creating `threads[1..N-1]`, it dereferences `nullptr` → **Segmentation Fault**! *(Seen in 2024–25 Q3, 2022–23 Q3 & Q4, Ch5 Slide 44.)*

**The Fix — `PcoSemaphore startWall(0)`:**
1. Every worker calls `startWall.acquire();` at the very top of its function.
2. `main()` finishes the **entire** creation loop first, then calls `startWall.release();` **`N` times** (one token per thread).

> [!NOTE]
> **Two-Loop Init Alternative:** If workers only read a shared **data** array (like `theVector[i]` in `TheClass`, 2023–24 Q5) and never touch `threads[]`, you don't even need a semaphore—just allocate `theVector[i]` in a first `for` loop **before** spawning `PcoThread`s in a second `for` loop.

blocks.title: Starting Wall Pattern vs. Turnstile Alternative

annotations.note: Blocks until main() releases N tokens. (Turnstile alternative: main() calls release() once, and each worker does acquire(); release();).
Must release N times (once per waiting thread), NOT once!

blocks.title: Trick #2: Stack Lifetime & Cooperative Stop Traps
blocks.content:
* **Never let a local variable die before `join()`:** If `function1()` creates `MyClass obj;` on the stack and passes `std::ref(obj)` to a `PcoThread`, `function1()` **must** call `thread.join()` before returning—otherwise `obj` is destroyed while the thread still uses it! *(2021–22 Q3)*
* **Never `delete` or read results before `join()`:** Always `join()` all worker threads before printing shared results (`prime`) or calling `delete threads[i]`. *(2024–25 Q3)*
* **The `void should_stop()` Trap:** Putting `return;` inside a `void should_stop()` helper only returns from `should_stop()`, **not** from the worker loop! Make `should_stop()` return `bool` and write `if (should_stop()) return;` inside the worker function. *(2024–25 Q3)*

sections.title: 2. Mutex Patterns & Traps (`PcoMutex`)
sections.description: Early returns, performance optimization, dual-object locking, and read-check-write atomicity.

blocks.title: 4 Essential `PcoMutex` Tricks
blocks.content:
1. **Unlock Before EVERY Early `return`:** In methods like `LinkedList::push_front`, `pop_front`, or `get` *(2024–25 Q4)*, if you `lock()` at the top, you **must** `unlock()` before every `return;` / `return 0;` / `return -1;`—missing even one path causes an immediate permanent deadlock.
2. **Never Declare a `PcoMutex` as a Local Variable (`PCO_4_mutex.pdf` p. 43):** Declaring `PcoMutex m;` inside a thread function creates a separate mutex on each thread's stack—providing **zero** mutual exclusion. It must be `static`, global, or a shared class member.
3. **Local-Copy Trick for Heavy Work (`AlmostGreat`, 2023–24 Q1):** Never hold a mutex during slow computations (`someHugeFunction`) or `new`/`delete` if you don't need to:
   ```cpp
   m_mutex.lock();
   double localA = m_a; // snapshot under lock
   m_mutex.unlock();    // release BEFORE heavy work!
   return someHugeFunction(localA);
   ```
4. **Lock Ordering + Self-Check for Dual Objects (`Player`, 2022–23 Q4):** When a method locks both `this` and `other` (`attack`/`heal`), AND in cross-resource locking (`semA` + `semB`, 2021–22 Q2):
   * **Self-check first (in both `lockPair` AND `unlockPair`!):** If `a == b`, lock **once** and unlock **once**! (Locking twice = self-deadlock on `PcoMutex`; unlocking twice on a `PcoSemaphore(1)` bumps its counter to `2` and breaks mutual exclusion!)
   * **Global lock order:** Always lock the lower `id` (or lower pointer address, or `semA` before `semB`) first—eliminates circular-wait deadlocks.
5. **Keep Read-Check-Write in ONE Critical Section:** Never `unlock()` between reading a shared variable and writing it back (`threadB` in 2022–23 Q2); another thread can modify it in between!

blocks.title: Deadlock-Free Dual-Object Locking Template

annotations.note: Prevents self-deadlock if a player targets itself (e.g., heal(this)).
Consistent global order (lower id first) makes circular wait impossible.
If using PcoSemaphore(1), releasing twice when a == b would bump the semaphore to 2 and break mutual exclusion!

sections.title: 3. The 4 Universal `PcoSemaphore` Patterns
sections.description: Gatekeeper + state guard, weighted resource pools, task graphs, and avoiding semaphore traps.

blocks.title: Pattern A: Gatekeeper + State Guard (`PontLevant`, `DepartCourse`, `RacletteTic`)
blocks.content:
Whenever threads must wait for a **condition** (bridge lowered, starting gun fired, group of 5 ready, 1 PER + 3 students ready), use this exact skeleton:

* `PcoSemaphore mutex(1);` — protects the state booleans/counters (`estAbaisse`, `nbWaiting`).
* `PcoSemaphore waitSem(0);` — the waiting room.

**The Golden Rule of Gatekeepers:**
> **ALWAYS call `mutex.release()` BEFORE calling `waitSem.acquire()`!**
> If you block on `waitSem.acquire()` while still holding `mutex`, no other thread can enter `abaisse()` / `coupDeFeu()` / `racleur()` to wake you up → **guaranteed deadlock**!

And when waking threads while holding `mutex`, release **only** `nbWaiting` tokens (resetting `nbWaiting = 0`) so idempotent calls (`abaisse()` called twice) never leave phantom extra tokens in `waitSem`!

blocks.title: Pattern B: Weighted Pool (`Votations`), Pattern C: Task Graph (`T0`–`T6`) & Common Traps
blocks.content:
* **Pattern B — Weighted Resource Pool (`Votations`, 2021–22 Q5):**
  If a thread needs `k` units from `semVoix(N)` via a loop `for (i = 0..k-1) semVoix.acquire();`, two threads acquiring `k` simultaneously can each grab half the tokens and **deadlock**! Fix: wrap the `acquire()` loop in an outer `mutexEntre(1)`, while `sort()` calls `semVoix.release()` **without** touching `mutexEntre`.
* **Pattern C — Task Dependency Graph (`T0`–`T6`, 2022–23 Q6):**
  Give each task `Ti` a `PcoSemaphore semTi(0);`. After `Ti` finishes, it calls `semTi.release()` once for **each outgoing arrow**. Before `Tj` starts, it calls `semTi.acquire()` once for **each incoming arrow**.
* **Trap — `PcoSemaphore(-1)`:** Constructor takes `unsigned int n = 0`. Passing `-1` underflows to `UINT_MAX` and never blocks! *(2024–25 Q1e, 2023–24 Q4.3)*
* **Trap — Active-Waiting Order & Memory Fences *(2024–25 Q2, Ch4)*:** In Peterson-style algorithms, `intention[self] = true;` must happen **before** testing `intention[other]` or yielding `tour` (otherwise both threads can enter the CS simultaneously!). On multi-core CPUs, a `std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acq_rel)` is also required.
* **Trap — `rand()` is NOT thread-safe:** `rand()` uses hidden global state—protect it with a mutex or use thread-local RNG. *(2022–23 Q3 & Q4)*
* **Trap — `std::vector<bool>` & `double`:** `std::vector<bool>` packs 8 bits/byte (concurrent `vec[0]` and `vec[1]` race!), and 64-bit `double` writes aren't atomic on 32-bit CPUs.

blocks.question: In a gatekeeper class (`PontLevant`, `DepartCourse`, `PrinterManager`), what happens if a thread calls `waitSem.acquire()` BEFORE calling `mutex.release()`?
options: Guaranteed deadlock if the condition is false: the thread sleeps while holding `mutex`, blocking any thread that tries to signal it.
A spurious wakeup occurs, waking the thread twice.
blocks.correct_answer: Guaranteed deadlock if the condition is false: the thread sleeps while holding `mutex`, blocking any thread that tries to signal it.
blocks.explanation: `PcoSemaphore::acquire()` does NOT release other mutexes or semaphores (unlike a monitor/condition variable's `wait()`). If a thread blocks on `waitSem.acquire()` while still holding `mutex`, any thread calling `abaisse()`/`giveBack()`/`coupDeFeu()` will block on `mutex.acquire()` forever.
